design_detail: Retraction notice, not a study: a letter headed 'Retraction' in Science 2003;301:1479 (12 September 2003), by Ricaurte, Yuan, Hatzidimitriou, Cord and McCann, withdrawing their report of severe dopaminergic neurotoxicity in primates after a common recreational dose regimen of MDMA (Science 2002;297:2260-2263). About 600 words, no data tables. The brief asked for a card of design 'commentary'; the schema has no such value, so 'narrative-review' is used, as for the three 2024 retraction notices already carded, and the choice is flagged for the senior author's open decision on a design for notices (SENIOR-DECISIONS item 29(5)).
can_establish: That the 2002 report was retracted by its authors on 12 September 2003; the reason they gave (a labelling error, so that all but one animal received methamphetamine rather than MDMA); the evidence they give for it (analyses of frozen brains from two animals that died and of the bottle labelled methamphetamine, by three independent laboratories, with gas chromatography-mass spectrometry); the sequence that led them to check (failure to extend the finding to oral dosing, then failure to reproduce it with a new batch of authenticated MDMA); and what the authors say the error does and does not call into question.
cannot_establish: What any animal in the study actually received beyond the labelling error (the original sample was depleted and the bottle labelled MDMA discarded); which animal received MDMA or what it showed; whether other publications from the same supply were affected; whether MDMA damages dopamine neurons in primates or people, which the notice explicitly leaves open; and whether any institutional investigation followed, which the notice does not mention.

exposure.measurement: The notice reports the exposure checks done after publication: gas chromatography-mass spectrometry of brains frozen from two animals that died shortly after dosing, and of the bottle labelled '(+)-methamphetamine HCl', each by three independent laboratories.

outcomes.instruments: Gas chromatography-mass spectrometry and other analytical techniques, as described in the notice.
outcomes.operationalization: The outcome is the identity of the compound given.

analysis.selective_reporting: The notice does not say which animal received MDMA, what that animal showed, how many animals were in each affected study, whether other publications used the same supply, or whether any investigation followed.

interpretation_gap.results_show: The authors withdraw the 2002 report because the drug given to all but one animal came from a bottle labelled MDMA that contained methamphetamine, established by analysis of two animals' brains, which contained methamphetamine and amphetamine and no trace of MDMA or MDA, and of the bottle labelled methamphetamine, which was found to contain MDMA.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The notice states that the labelling error does not call into question earlier studies of the serotonin neurotoxic potential of MDMA in several species, that dose regimens in the range used by some people but not yet tested might still produce dopamine neurotoxicity in primates as they do in rodents, that lasting effects of MDMA on dopaminergic function in humans have been reported and that some people with a history of MDMA use have developed parkinsonism, and that the possibility remains uncertain until it can be examined more fully. These are the authors' own statements about what remains open, not findings.

timeline.event: The report is published in Science (27 September) and widely covered
Published criticism and reply in Science (6 June), three months before the retraction
Case study of newspaper coverage: 26 of 50 large US newspapers covered the publication and 20 the retraction

replication.where_it_stands: The retraction stands; the 2002 report is cited only to document it (METHODS §3.2). The notice's own statement that the dopamine question in primates remains open has not been resolved by any later primate study read for this page.

funding.funder: Not stated in the notice; the retracted report was funded by US Public Health Service grants.
funding.affiliations_note: Departments of Neurology, Neurosciences and Psychiatry, Johns Hopkins Bayview Medical Center.

what_would_settle_it: For the record itself, nothing further is needed. For the open question the notice names, a new primate study with independently verified drug, pre-specified outcomes and blinded assessment, and a systematic search of human dopamine imaging since 2003.

domains.note: Not a review: the notice reports the authors' own withdrawal of one paper, so nothing is selected.
The notice asserts that earlier serotonin studies are unaffected and cites them, but gives no account of which other work used the same supply or over what period.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: The authors are the authors of the retracted paper and of most of the work they say is unaffected.

The analytical findings are stated plainly, but the closing paragraph adds unquantified statements about lasting dopaminergic effects in humans and cases of parkinsonism, citing references not examined here.

domains.domain: Balance of the account of what the error affects (the possibility that other work was affected is under-represented)
domains.note: The notice says the error does not call the serotonin literature into question, without describing how far the mislabelled supply reached.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to a retraction notice; the editors' narrative-review checklist is used as the closest available, its domains read as questions about the notice as a source. It is the primary record of the retraction and its stated grounds and may be cited for both; its claims about what the error leaves untouched are the authors' own.

key_findings.finding: The authors retract their 2002 report after discovering that the drug used to treat all but one animal came from a bottle that contained (+)-methamphetamine instead of the intended (+/-)MDMA, and note that methamphetamine would be expected to produce the combined dopaminergic and serotonergic pattern they reported.
The retracted report drew on studies done in their laboratory over about 2 years in two species of non-human primates.

The sequence that led to the discovery: they could not extend the dopamine finding to oral dosing; repeated attempts to reproduce it with systemically given MDMA identical to the original regimen failed under a variety of conditions; they then noticed that the failed replications used a new batch of MDMA, authenticated by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry.

Laboratory records showed that the two bottles had been requested from the supplier on the same date, were for the same amount (10 g), were processed by the supplier on the same day and delivered on the same day with different affixed labels, the same delivery reference number and different batch numbers; both were stored in their original containers in a locked safe.
When the bottle labelled '(+)-methamphetamine HCl' was analysed by three independent laboratories, it was found to consist of MDMA with no evidence of even trace amounts of methamphetamine.

The original sample was depleted and the empty bottle labelled MDMA discarded; frozen brains from two animals that died shortly after dosing were analysed by three independent laboratories and contained methamphetamine and its metabolite amphetamine, neither of which is a metabolite of MDMA, with no trace of MDMA or MDA.

Review of the laboratory records showed that all but one animal in the study had been treated with drug from the bottle labelled MDMA, which had been processed on the same date as the bottle labelled methamphetamine.
key_findings.note: The notice does not identify the one animal that received MDMA or report what that animal showed.

key_findings.finding: The authors state that the labelling error does not call into question earlier studies demonstrating the serotonin neurotoxic potential of MDMA in several species, including non-human primates.

They add that it remains possible that dose regimens in the range of those used by some people, but different from those tested so far, produce dopamine neurotoxicity in primates as they do in rodents; that lasting effects of MDMA on dopaminergic function in humans have recently been reported and that some people with a history of MDMA use have developed parkinsonism; and that the possibility remains uncertain until the dopamine neurotoxic potential of MDMA in primates can be examined more fully.
key_findings.note: The supporting citations (their references 9-14) were not read here; the statement is recorded as the authors' own.

reporting_issues.issue: The notice does not say which animal received MDMA, what that animal showed, or how many animals were affected in each of the studies spanning about 2 years.
reporting_issues.consequence: The one uncontaminated data point in the programme is unreported, so nothing survives from the report even in principle.

reporting_issues.issue: It asserts that earlier serotonin studies are unaffected without saying when the mislabelled supply was received or which other work used it.
reporting_issues.consequence: A reader cannot judge the scope of the error from the notice; a request for an investigation of the laboratory's work since the supply arrived is recorded in the media case study (card sc_barnett_2021), not here.

reporting_issues.issue: The notice gives no account of how the mislabelling arose at the supplier or in the laboratory beyond the delivery records, and names no corrective measure.
reporting_issues.consequence: It documents the error without documenting its handling; the project records it as the primary source for the fact and the stated grounds of the retraction only.

verification.source_read: PDF, p. 1479 (the whole notice, read in the text extraction and checked on the rendered page; the remaining pages of the PDF are unrelated Science letters and were not read)
